n: Solomon spends thirteen years building his own palace complex — almost twice as long as the seven years spent on the temple. The contrast may quietly hint at shifting priorities.
The “House of the Forest of Lebanon,” about 150 by 75 feet, was named for its many cedar pillars, which made the hall feel like a forest. It served as a royal hall and armory.

f.w: the house of the forest of Lebanon

n: Its cedar roof rested on forty-five beams or pillars, arranged fifteen to a row.
Windows were set in three rows, facing each other across the hall.
Its doorways and frames were rectangular, with windows facing each other in three tiers.
He also built a colonnade, or Hall of Pillars, about 75 by 45 feet, with a porch and canopy in front.
He built the Hall of Judgment, where his throne stood and he decided cases — the place where wisdom like that shown in chapter 3 would be exercised. It was paneled in cedar.
His private residence stood in another courtyard behind the hall. He also built a similar palace for his Egyptian wife, Pharaoh’s daughter.
All these buildings used expensive cut stone, sawn to measure and finished inside and out, from foundation to top.

f.g: The top course of a wall.

n: The foundations were enormous blocks, some 12 to 15 feet long.
Above the foundations were more fine cut stones and cedar beams.
The great courtyard, like the temple’s inner court, was walled with three rows of cut stone and a row of cedar beams.

f.w: three rows of hewed stones, and a row of cedar beams

n: For the temple’s bronze work, Solomon brings a master craftsman named Hiram (also called Huram) from Tyre — not the king of the same name.
Hiram’s mother was an Israelite widow and his father a Tyrian bronze worker. Like Bezaleel, who built the tabernacle, he was filled with wisdom and skill for sacred work.

f.w: a widow's son of the tribe of Naphtali
f.g: Chronicles says his mother was from Dan; she may have been of Dan by birth and married into Naphtali, or the reverse.

n: He casts two great bronze pillars, each about 27 feet tall and 18 feet around.
Each pillar is topped with a cast bronze capital about 7.5 feet high.

f.g: Capitals — the decorative tops of columns.

n: The capitals are decorated with lattice networks and chain-like wreaths, seven on each.
Two rows of bronze pomegranates encircle each capital over the latticework.

f.g: Pomegranates, full of seeds, symbolized fruitfulness and also decorated the high priest’s robe.

n: The upper parts of the capitals in the porch are shaped like lilies, about 6 feet high.

f.g: Lily or lotus designs — symbols of life and beauty.

n: Two hundred pomegranates in rows circle each capital, above the rounded bulge next to the latticework.

f.g: The rounded, bowl-shaped part of the capital.

n: The pillars stand at the temple entrance and receive names: Jachin (“He will establish”) and Boaz (“In Him is strength”). Together they proclaim that God establishes His house and gives it strength.

f.g: “In Him is strength” — also the name of David’s ancestor (Ruth 4:21).

n: With the lily designs on top, the pillars are finished.
Hiram casts a huge round bronze basin, the “molten sea,” 15 feet across and 7.5 feet high. The priests used it for washing.

f.g: A massive cast-metal basin; Chronicles says it was for the priests to wash in.
A rounded figure for the circumference.

n: Two rows of gourd-shaped ornaments, cast in one piece with the basin, run around it under the rim.

f.g: Gourd-shaped knobs; Chronicles describes them as oxen-like figures.

n: The sea rests on twelve bronze oxen, three facing each direction — perhaps representing the twelve tribes. Baptismal fonts in Latter-day Saint temples follow this pattern, resting on twelve oxen.
The basin’s walls are a handbreadth thick, its rim flared like a cup or lily blossom. It held around 11,000 gallons.

f.g: A bath was about 5.8 gallons (22 liters); 2 Chronicles 4:5 gives 3,000.

n: Hiram also makes ten bronze carts or stands, each about 6 feet square and 4.5 feet high, to carry water basins.
The stands are built with panels set between frames.
The panels are decorated with lions, oxen, and cherubim, with hanging wreaths or garlands below.

f.g: Garlands or wreaths of hammered metal.

n: Each stand has four bronze wheels and axles, with supports at the corners to hold the basin.
The opening on top of each stand, made to hold a basin, is round, with square-paneled engravings around it.
The wheels, about 27 inches high, are under the panels, with axles attached to the stand.
They are built like chariot wheels — axles, hubs, rims, and spokes, all cast in bronze.
Each stand has four corner supports cast as part of the stand itself.
A round band about 9 inches high runs around the top, with supports and panels cast in one piece.
Cherubim, lions, and palm trees are engraved wherever there is space, surrounded by wreaths.
All ten stands are cast alike, identical in size and shape.

f.w: one casting, one measure, and one size
f.g: Uniform craftsmanship — order and harmony in God’s house.

n: Ten bronze basins, each holding about 230 gallons, sit on the stands. Chronicles says they were used to rinse the parts of burnt offerings.
Five stands are placed on each side of the temple, and the great sea at the southeast corner.
Hiram also makes the smaller items — basins, shovels for ashes, and sprinkling bowls — completing his work for the temple.

f.g: Used to remove ashes from the altar.

n: A summary of Hiram’s work begins: the two pillars with their bowl-shaped capitals and the latticework covering them.
The four hundred pomegranates — two rows for each lattice on the capitals.
The ten stands and their ten basins.
The great sea and the twelve oxen beneath it.
All the pots, shovels, and bowls, made of burnished bronze.
These items were cast in clay molds in the Jordan Valley, where the clay soil was ideal for metal casting.

f.g: Towns in the Jordan Valley; archaeologists have found evidence of ancient metalworking in this region.

n: There was so much bronze that it was never weighed — the amount could not be calculated.

f.w: neither was the weight of the brass found out

n: Solomon also made the golden furnishings for inside the temple: the golden incense altar and the table for the bread of the Presence.

f.g: Bread of the Presence — twelve loaves set before the Lord continually.

n: Ten lampstands of pure gold stood before the inner sanctuary, five on each side, with golden flower decorations, lamps, and tongs.
Even the smallest tools — bowls, wick trimmers, basins, ladles, firepans — and the door hinges for both rooms were made of gold. Nothing in God’s house was too small to matter.

f.g: Firepans for carrying coals and burning incense.

n: The work is complete. Solomon brings in the silver, gold, and articles David had dedicated and stores them in the temple treasury, honoring his father’s preparations.

f.w: the things which David his father had dedicated
